name: PT Ancara Logistics Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Ancara Logistics: a captive coal barge operator priced as a growth stock
frontmatter.summary: Ancara's Q3-2026 LK confirms a sharp revenue step-down and a thin operating quarter; related-party interest, not the fleet, carried pre-tax profit. We roll the model to the nine-month actuals, hold the weak run-rate into Q4 and widen the loan-book haircut to a fifth. The HSC/IHSG exit on 2 November is an index-flow event already in our konglo lens, not a change in value; OJK's criminal-action statement names DSSA/BREN/CUAN, not ALII. The shares still trade far above fundamental value; REDUCE.
thesis: The business is captive: revenue from two affiliated miners dominates, and the same parties are the counterparties on a large non-current receivable that now generates much of pre-tax profit.

The Q3-2026 LK confirms the step-down: nine-month revenue of IDR701.5bn leaves a third quarter far below the prior year, and the quarter's gross margin fell sharply; management has not given a sourced explanation, so our base case holds the weak run-rate into Q4.

Operating cash flow is real but working capital absorbs a large share of it, and the related-party loan book now generates most of pre-tax profit; in Q3 interest and penalty income exceeded operating profit.
We value the logistics operations on discounted cash flow and the loan book at a haircut to book value; together they sit well below the market price.
The shares carry a high-shareholding-concentration regime premium; our target keeps part of that premium for the next twelve months and still implies a negative total return.

catalysts.event: HSC-designated shares leave the IHSG calculation; IDX says the index level is unaffected
FY2026 audited results and dividend declaration (expected)
MSCI decision on Indonesia market classification

blocks.text: **What changed.** The Q3-2026 LK is now in the pack and we have rolled the model to it. Nine-month revenue of IDR701.5bn leaves a third-quarter run-rate roughly half the prior-year quarter, and the quarter's gross margin fell well below the nine-month average; the nine-month figures flatter the trend. The data pack's third-quarter operating-profit and operating-expense lines do not reconcile to the LK — nine-month operating profit of IDR251.8bn less the first-half IDR233.2bn leaves a materially larger quarter than the pack shows — so we use the LK-derived economics and have flagged the pack to OPS. Management has still not explained the step-down in the filings we hold. We hold the weak Q3 run-rate into Q4. Separately, HSC-designated shares formally leave the IHSG calculation on Monday 2 November 2026 [S17]; that is an index-flow and marginal-buyer event, not a change in intrinsic value. The exclusion was already in our konglo lens and IDX says the index level is unaffected, so we do not double-count it; the stock-level liquidity risk is sized in the risk section. OJK's statement that DSSA/BREN/CUAN-type cases can proceed to criminal action [S16] is a regime reminder, not an ALII-specific finding; the registry records no enforcement against ALII. This revision also corrects two disclosure errors — the valuation section stated the industry's default method weights rather than the modelled ones, and the capex comparison understated the nine-month run-rate — and widens the related-party recovery haircut from ten to twenty per cent on the cash-collection evidence [S6]. The final review pass then fixed the method-weight rendering in this summary and the valuation section, aligned the prior-year interest-income restatement note with the pack and the filing, and deducted the related-party payable at face value in the valuation bridge so the loan book and its funding are shown on both sides [S5][S6]. The rating stays **REDUCE**; the target moves to Rp475 from the prior published level, just under a tenth lower, against a price of Rp605, a total return of -19.8% including the next twelve months' dividend of Rp11. The cut is almost entirely in the fundamental value, which falls by about a fifth from the version before the results roll: FY2027E revenue now ramps at 2.0% rather than the prior full-recovery rate because no filed affiliate tonnage contract supports it [S6]; the EV/EBITDA leg is down-weighted to a cross-check at 10%; and the related-party bridge now carries an eighty per cent recovery probability [S6]. Our fundamental twelve-month value is Rp215; the gap is the regime lens, not a business view, set out in the valuation section below.

The company is a coal-logistics operator — barges, tugs, a floating transhipment unit and a coal terminal — founded in 2019 to move coal for two affiliated miners, PT Ade Putra Tanrajeng and PT Guruh Putra Bersama [S4]. The affiliation is not incidental: related-party customers supplied IDR639.2bn of the IDR970.2bn of FY2025 revenue from the largest of them alone [S5], and the company also carries a non-current receivable from related parties of IDR1,262.8bn at the end of 9M 2026 [S6]. Related-party interest and penalty income on those balances reached IDR169.0bn of pre-tax support in FY2025, on our restated presentation [S5].

Our variant view is that the Q3-2026 step-down is better treated as the new run-rate until the company explains it, and that the related-party interest income is a financing return on a loan book we value separately, not an operating multiple. We value the fleet on through-cycle cash flows and the loan book at a haircut to book value, and we let the weak recent quarter set the near-term volume base.

Three things move the value. First, whether the affiliated miners restore the volumes and rates that produced the FY2025 revenue base [S5]. Second, whether the related-party receivable is serviced in cash or continues to accrete; in Q3 the interest and penalty income exceeded operating profit, so the loan book, not the fleet, carried pre-tax profit [S6]. Third, the regime: the shares sit on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, and the exchange's disclosure shows only three holders at or above five per cent while the public, each below five per cent, holds 20.2% [S6]. The registry's market-convention free float of 19.4% is a slightly narrower measure than that public table, and both clear the fifteen per cent minimum. The 2 November IHSG formalisation is already inside the lens [S17]; it is a flow and marginal-buyer event, not a change in intrinsic value. The price today is 3.0x today's engine fundamental value of Rp199.

Ancara is a young company built around a single coal group. Its economics are those of a haulage
contractor: it is paid a rate per tonne moved, bears fuel and crew costs, and must keep financing
receivables while it waits to be paid. When the customer and the shareholder are the same family, the
working-capital cycle becomes a governance question as much as an operational one.

Ancara runs two reported segments. Coal barging and floating loading earned IDR641.4bn of segment revenue in FY2025 against IDR690.7bn a year earlier, while the loading-unloading segment (the ACT coal terminal and stevedoring) earned IDR328.9bn [S5]. The barging segment carries the fleet; the loading segment earns the higher gross margin because its cost base is a terminal rather than fuel and charter-in [S5].

The revenue model is a per-tonne service contract, not a commodity sale. Ancara is paid to move coal from the mine's loading point to the transhipment or stockpile node, and the customer bears the coal price risk while Ancara bears utilisation, fuel and crew risk [S4]. That distinction matters for the model: a coal price rise does not lift Ancara's margin directly, but it does lift the affiliated miners' willingness to produce and therefore the tonnage on offer [S11]. The direct cost exposure is fuel, and the notes show it recovered through the per-tonne rate [S5][S6].

The fleet is the asset base: the April 2026 BRI investment-credit disclosure lists 43.0 units barges, two tugboats and one floating transhipment unit as collateral, alongside the company's coal terminal and support vessels [S10]. Gross fixed assets are dominated by barges and the floating transhipment unit, depreciated over twenty and sixteen years respectively, with tugs over ten [S5]. Employees are few — the workforce is a vessel crew and a small head office in Bakrie Tower, Jakarta [S4].

Strategy is capacity-led. The company raised IPO proceeds in 2024, refinanced its Mandiri facilities with BRI in April 2026, and carries a dedicated capex tranche to buy or build twenty tugboats and six barges, with a grace period matching the build contract [S10]. It also bought PT Ancara Transshipment Services from an affiliate in September 2025 for IDR29.7bn, consolidating a transhipment capability it had previously hired [S8][S5].

Operating leverage is high in both directions. Once a vessel is committed to a coal run, the crew, fuel and charter-in costs arrive whether or not the barge sails full, so a fall in tonnage hits revenue before it hits cost [S5]. That is what the Q3-2026 numbers show: revenue fell, the quarter's gross margin fell with it, and the SG&A ratio rose because head-office and terminal costs do not flex with volume [S6]. The same structure works in reverse when the affiliated mines lift output, which is why we treat volume recovery as the single most important swing factor rather than an input among many.

The customer base is the defining feature. Two related parties, PT Ade Putra Tanrajeng and PT Guruh Putra Bersama, are the group's affiliated coal mines and the reason the company exists [S4]. Third- party customers such as PT Rwood Resources Indonesia are growing but remain secondary [S5]. We classify Ancara as a captive logistics provider rather than an independent barging operator: the relationship secures volume in a downturn and caps pricing in an upturn.

Indonesian coal logistics is a derivative of coal output and of the distance between mine gate and barge loading point. The coal deck we carry puts high-calorific thermal coal at US$150.3 spot with a forward marker of US$118.0 for FY2027. The government's monthly reference price for high-calorific coal sits below the Newcastle spot, and the October 2026 print is below its July level, so the mid-year high has not been regained [S11].

The demand driver is therefore mine output, not the price directly: a miner that cuts its plan moves fewer tonnes whatever the price. That matters here because the affiliated mines are the customers. The supply side is barge availability, and the barrier is capital — a barge fleet is long-lived and expensive, and financing it requires contracted volume, which is exactly what a captive relationship provides [S10].

The chain Ancara serves has three links. Coal leaves the mine by road to a river loading point; it is loaded onto a barge or a floating transhipment unit; and it is finally discharged at a stockpile or a mother vessel [S4]. Ancara participates in the middle and final links — barging and floating loading on one side, the ACT terminal's barge-to-stockpile handling on the other [S4]. The segment split follows that geography: the floating loading and barging work is where the fleet is deployed, and the terminal is a fixed asset that earns a handling fee on whatever tonnage passes through it [S5]. Integrating the terminal and the transhipment unit was the logic of the PT Ancara Transshipment Services purchase, which moved a capability the company had previously hired in-house [S8].

Volume is the binding constraint on industry economics. The government's monthly reference price sets the revenue pool for the miners, and the October 2026 print remains below the July high [S11]; when the reference price is firm, the affiliated miners have both the cash and the incentive to sustain output, and logistics demand follows. When it softens, the first response is usually to trim the mine plan rather than the stripping ratio, and the tonnage offered to barging contractors falls ahead of the coal price itself. That is the mechanism behind the Q3 2026 step-down in the company's own revenue and the reason we watch the reference price as a leading indicator for volume rather than as a direct revenue driver [S6][S11].

Competition is fragmented: independent barge owners, coal traders with their own fleets and the miners' in-house logistics arms all compete for tonnage. We see no durable moat beyond the captive contracts, no pricing power against the affiliates, and no evidence of a cost advantage that survives a fuel-price swing. On the five forces, buyer power is very high because two related customers dominate the book [S5], supplier power is moderate in fuel and charter markets [S5], new entry is capital-constrained but not barred because the fleet can be financed against contracted volume [S10], and rivalry is intensifying as coal volumes flatten. The company does not disclose market share or third-party rates, so we cannot test whether it earns a premium rate; the disclosure we hold is consistent with a service provider that is paid a contracted rate and collects it slowly [S5][S6].

Barging on Indonesian rivers is a commodity service with low switching costs for the customer and high
fixed costs for the operator. The usual defensible positions are a captive mine relationship, a
terminal at a bottleneck, or a fleet large enough to guarantee delivery during peak season. A company
with one of the three is a contractor; a company with all three has a moat. Ancara has the first and
is building the third.

Regulation touches the company indirectly: coal export rules, the domestic market obligation and the royalty regime set the miners' economics and therefore their logistics budgets. We found no company-specific licence that changes the picture; the company's own permits are shipping licences (SIUPAL), safety-management certification and terminal operating approvals [S4].

FY2025 revenue was IDR970.2bn with a gross margin of 45.4% and EBITDA of IDR425.5bn after our restatement of depreciation from the notes [S5]. The reported operating profit of IDR359.6bn is reproduced faithfully; the data pack's depreciation is not, because the Indonesian cash-flow statement is prepared on the direct method and carries no depreciation back-add. We take IDR65.9bn of depreciation from the fixed-asset and right-of-use notes and use it for the whole history [S5].

Cost of revenue is dominated by subcontracted freight, fuel, charter-in rentals and depreciation, in that order [S5]. Fuel was a little over a fifth of cost of revenue in FY2025, so a Brent move matters, but the 9M 2026 gross margin held at the prior-year level even as Brent rose, which tells us the cost is recovered through the per-tonne rate rather than absorbed. We model full fuel pass-through and hold the last actual gross margin.

The 9M 2026 figures are the important new information. Revenue of IDR701.5bn compares with IDR970.2bn for FY2025, and the first half alone was IDR579.7bn [S12][S6]. The arithmetic leaves a Q3-2026 revenue run-rate roughly half the prior-year quarter, using nine-month 2025 revenue of IDR764.7bn against the first-half 2025 figure of IDR544.9bn. Nine-month gross profit of IDR318.2bn less the first-half IDR281.0bn leaves a third-quarter gross margin far below the nine-month average. Nine-month operating profit of IDR251.8bn less the first-half IDR233.2bn leaves a thin third-quarter operating profit; the data pack's third-quarter operating-profit and operating-expense lines do not reconcile to that LK arithmetic, so we use the LK-derived figures and have flagged the pack to OPS. Nine-month pre-tax profit of IDR393.7bn less the first-half IDR349.5bn leaves a third-quarter pre-tax figure supported mainly by interest and penalty income: nine-month interest and penalty income of IDR124.6bn less the first-half IDR86.0bn exceeded the quarter's operating profit. The loan book, not the fleet, carried the quarter. Management has not, in the filings we hold, explained the step-down; our FY2026E is the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter run-rate, and does not assume an immediate recovery [S6][S12].

On that build FY2026E revenue is IDR823.3bn, the gross margin 43.1% and EBIT IDR270.5bn. Against the published FY2026E build, revenue is in line by construction because that build already used the nine-month LK; the new information is the Q3 margin and the composition of profit, both weaker than the nine-month average. We have cut the FY2026E gross margin and raised the opex and working-capital ratios accordingly [S6][S12]. The FY2026E EBITDA margin sits below FY2025's because Q4 is held at the Q3 run-rate; that is the sourced actual, not a cautious haircut [S6][S12]. On the house calibration test the FY2026E Ebitda margin sits a few points below FY2025A: the gap is the Q3-2026 trough (nine-month gross profit of IDR318.2bn less the first-half IDR281.0bn leaves a weak third quarter on IDR701.5bn nine-month revenue, [S6][S12]) carried into Q4, it is inside the engine's five-point tolerance, and FY2028E restores the FY2025 gross margin only once the revenue ramp is complete. The intra-year path is therefore explicit: Q4-2026 is the trough, FY2027E grows 2.0% as utilisation improves, and FY2028E grows 8.0% to complete the recovery. No filed tonnage contract sources the affiliate volume behind that path; the twenty-six-vessel BRI tranche is capacity, not contracted tonnage [S10], and management has not explained the step-down [S6]. The fourth-quarter hold is the largest single conservative input: if Q4-2026 were at the nine-month average instead of the Q3 run-rate, FY2026E revenue and the twelve-month value would both be higher, and the revenue-growth axis of the sensitivity grid in the valuation section shows the value effect. We keep the hold because the Q3 actual is the latest sourced economics and no filing explains it, not as a default haircut [S6][S12].

Cash conversion is the second issue. FY2025 operating cash flow was well below net profit because receivables grew faster than revenue, but 9M 2026 operating cash flow of IDR278.6bn was strong: cash receipts from customers ran ahead of revenue as trade receivables fell [S6]. The third quarter alone generated the bulk of it, with nine-month operating cash flow of IDR278.6bn against IDR19.1bn in the first half. Operating working capital was IDR371.5bn at FY2025; at 30 September 2026 it was higher on a lower revenue base, and we hold that ratio rather than assume a release [S6]. On top of it sits the non-current related-party loan book of IDR1,262.8bn [S6], which we value separately as a financing asset.

Capex in 9M 2026 is already at the FY2025 full-year level: nine-month capex of IDR104.5bn compares with IDR31.9bn in the first half, so the third quarter carried the bulk of the build under the BRI capex tranche [S5][S6][S10]. Debt has been refinanced at a fixed rate well below the legacy Mandiri cost [S10], so finance charges of IDR34.5bn in FY2025 were far below the prior year [S5]. The dividend policy allows up to four-fifths of net profit after capex and working capital [S3]; the FY2025 dividend of IDR205.7bn, a DPS of Rp13, was paid in 9M 2026, while the cash-flow line of IDR71.2bn is the prior year's dividend [S6]. The capex is replacement and fleet renewal plus capacity whose incremental tonnage is not separately sourced; the bull case is where the new tugs and barges earn from the second half of FY2027 [S10]. Dividend capacity is the market's anchor for this sector: at the modelled payout of 55.0% the FY2026E yield is 1.7%; at the policy ceiling of four-fifths [S3] it would be proportionally higher but still below our cost of equity, so the ceiling is a bull input, not the base case.
Earnings-quality assessment, per the house screen:

items: **Accruals.** The gap between net profit and operating cash flow narrowed sharply in 9M 2026, but the
profit base now includes a large non-cash interest accrual on related-party balances, and in Q3 that
accrual exceeded operating profit. We treat it as non-operating in the model.
**Receivables versus revenue.** Related-party trade receivables fell in 9M 2026 as cash was
collected, but they remain large relative to revenue, and the non-current related-party receivable
rose from IDR1,160.9bn to IDR1,262.8bn [S6] — a divergence flag.
**Related-party gravity.** Related-party revenue is the majority of the top line [S5], and the
non-current related-party receivable is close to half of total assets [S6]. In Q3 the interest and
penalty income carried pre-tax profit. This is the modal value-destruction channel on this exchange,
and it is disclosed rather than hidden; we classify it as an optics-and-governance flag, not a
manipulation-class finding.
**Structure.** The name sits on the high-shareholding-concentration list; the controlling interest
and affiliates hold almost everything, with the public (each below five per cent) at
20.2% [S6]. The FY2025 statements carry a prior-period restatement of equity [S5]; we flag it and use the
restated figures.
**Board and notation.** No special notation or going-concern flag was found in the documents we
registered; we did not obtain the auditor's report text itself.

blocks.text: We use the industry method set: discounted cash flow to the firm at 70%, EV/EBITDA at 10% and price-to-book at 20%. A logistics operator with a contracted tonnage base and a long-lived fleet is best valued on cash flow; the multiple and book cross-checks test whether the market is paying for the earnings stream or the asset base. The weight on the EV/EBITDA leg is deliberately below the industry default because the engine applies the peer median to the last actual year's peak EBITDA, as explained below.

Our cost of equity is built from the Indonesian risk-free rate, a mature-market premium plus a country premium, and a relevered beta. The engine sets the pre-tax cost of debt at the risk-free rate plus a default spread, 9.4%, not the sourced fixed BRI facility rate [S10]; the sourced rate is lower, so the WACC is if anything conservative, and we have not overridden the engine's default. The resulting weighted average cost of capital is 12.5%.

The primary method discounts free cash flow to the firm over a ten-year horizon with a terminal growth rate of 3.5%. Working capital is the swing factor: at the 9M 2026 ratio, growth consumes cash before it produces it. The DCF values the enterprise at IDR2,770.6bn; after net debt and minorities, and after adding the net related-party bridge, it gives Rp207 per share. That figure already includes the related-party receivable in the bridge at its recovery probability, so the operating business alone is the smaller part; we do not add the receivable a second time. Net debt and minorities are struck on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet, consistent with the bridge [S6].

Two adjustments sit outside the operating cash flow. First, the non-current related-party receivable: it is a financing asset, not working capital, so we add it in the valuation bridge, sourced to the 9M 2026 balance sheet [S6], at a recovery probability the engine applies rather than at gross book value. We set that probability from the cash evidence: only IDR46.8bn of the IDR124.6bn interest and penalty accrued in 9M 2026 was received in cash [S6]; the loan book grew over the nine months [S6]; and part of the balance has no fixed repayment date, with maturities extended by amendment [S5]. The claim is contractual but unsecured, and only the group's continued servicing supports it, so we apply a twenty per cent haircut — an eighty per cent recovery — as the most likely outcome, not face value. The sensitivity is close to linear: the recovery assumption is the main swing factor between the DCF and the P/BV cross-check, and a fall to half of face value is the material downside, sized in the risk section. Second, the interest and penalty income it produces is included in our net-profit forecast but excluded from free cash flow, so the asset and its income are not counted twice. The IDR89.5bn due to related parties in non-current liabilities [S6] is a financing claim, not an operating balance: it is an affiliate loan that carries interest, plus balances due to the two controlling shareholders, and the filing routes movements in it through financing activities [S5][S6]. We therefore deduct it at face value as the second bridge item, so the receivable enters the bridge at its recovery probability and the payable leaves at book value, and the Rp207 DCF value already carries both sides of the related-party balance [S6].

The cross-checks diverge, and the divergence is informative. EV/EBITDA is 83.1% above the DCF at a multiple of 12.9x applied to LTM FY2025A EBITDA of IDR425.5bn: that is the cycle peak, about a third above the FY2026E IDR328.1bn, so for a cyclical in a step-down the leg is an optimistic bound rather than a base rate. We therefore weight it at 10% and give the DCF 70% and P/BV 20%. EBITDA capitalises the peak earnings base while the DCF charges the working-capital and capex needed to sustain it. The P/BV leg values the shares -21.9% relative to the DCF at 1.2x, because book equity carries the related-party receivable at face value while the DCF's bridge adds it once at its recovery probability; the book method therefore does the same job less precisely. That divergence is not noise: it tells us that the market's multiple is being paid for the earnings stream, not for the assets, and that a write-down of the receivable would move the P/BV cross-check far more than it would move the DCF. We weight the DCF accordingly and read the EV/EBITDA multiple as the optimistic bound and P/BV as the floor.

The 12.9x EV/EBITDA multiple is the median of the COAL_LOGISTICS peer set in the data pack — eleven names carry a usable multiple, including TEBE, MBSS, RMKE, TCPI, BESS and SGER — and that set spans from below five times to above forty, so the median is a fragile anchor [S0]. The DCF carries 70% for that reason; at a peer-low multiple the EV/EBITDA leg and the blended value would fall well below the target. The sensitivity grid shows the DCF; we have not added a bespoke multiple grid because the engine has no custom sensitivity axis, which we have flagged to OPS [S0].

The anchor statement: we value the name on through-cycle NAV, which the DCF expresses, while the market's anchor for coal logistics is dividend capacity. At the modelled payout the yield is 1.7%, below our cost of equity, so the market is not being paid to hold the premium the price embeds.

The Q4-2026 trough is the largest single conservative input in the forecast. The revenue-growth axis of the sensitivity grid shows the value effect: holding the fourth quarter at the nine-month average instead of the Q3 run-rate would move the twelve-month value toward the upper end of that axis, because the higher exit rate carries into every forecast year. We keep the trough hold because it is the latest sourced actual, not a default haircut [S6][S12].

What the price implies: a reverse DCF at today's Rp605 solves for the FY2027E revenue-growth assumption that lifts our DCF to the price. The required rate is 21.4% — a growth rate, not a cash-flow amount — against the 2.0% we model. That is beyond our bull scenario, not equal to it: the bull adds its mirrored growth and margin shock and still values the shares at Rp306 twelve months out against today's Rp605, so the price embeds a recovery that even the top of our range does not reach [S6].

The regime lens is separate from the business value. The price is 3.0x our fundamental value today, Rp199, and remains above our twelve-month fundamental value of Rp215: the two ratios are not contradictory, they are the same price against today's value and against the value twelve months out, and the lens bridges them. The only regime flag the lens applies to this name is the high-shareholding-concentration status: the free float of 19.4% is above the fifteen per cent minimum with no tier step due, the registry records no further index deletion and no OJK enforcement against ALII, and the HSC exclusion takes effect on 2 November 2026 [S17]; because the exclusion was already in the lens and IDX says the index level is unaffected, the formalisation is a calendar event, not a new value input. OJK's 2026 sanctions and its statement that DSSA/BREN/CUAN-type cases can proceed to criminal action [S15][S16] are a regime reminder; no ALII case is named, so they do not change the lens. Because there is no dated remediation step left that forces the premium to close quickly, the most likely path is slow drift rather than a step: the lens closes 35.0% of the log gap in the base regime, 75.0% in the bear and -10.0% in the bull. That produces the target of Rp475 against a fundamental value of Rp215. The 2 November IHSG exit is a flow event: it removes a marginal index buyer and can widen the discount at which the float trades, but it does not change the cash flows; no registered source discloses index-product holdings of ALII, so we do not size the flow. We are not shading the fundamental inputs to justify the price, and we are not treating the premium as value [S17].
**Downside risks**, with our likelihood and impact assessment:

items: **Customer concentration and volume loss — high likelihood, high impact.** Two related customers
dominate revenue, and the Q3-2026 run-rate already shows how quickly tonnage can disappear [S5][S6].
**Related-party receivable impairment — medium likelihood, very high impact.** A write-down of the
non-current balance would hit book equity and the bridge directly; the loans carry a high coupon and
an extended maturity, and interest is only partly collected in cash [S5][S6]. In Q3 the interest and
penalty income carried pre-tax profit, so an impairment would hit the earnings base as well as the
bridge. The bridge is IDR1,262.8bn against a DCF value of Rp207 per
share; a haircut of half would remove about a fifth of that DCF value, enough to take the
fundamental value toward the bear case. The bridge is already probability-weighted at the twenty per
cent recovery haircut described in the valuation section [S6], so the scenario table does not
stack a second write-down on top of it; the residual risk is that recovery falls below that
probability.
**Regime and liquidity — high likelihood, medium impact.** HSC shares leave the IHSG calculation
on 2 November 2026 [S17]; the exchange says the index arithmetic is unaffected, but the stock-level
flow is real. The float at risk is a fifth of the 15,825.8m shares — the
19.4% public float within a market capitalisation of
IDR9,574,609,000.00tn — against three-month average daily turnover of
IDR900.0m: clearing that float at recent turnover would take years of trading,
which is the stock-level discount risk, separate from the index-level neutrality. The formalisation
removes a marginal buyer; it is a flow and liquidity event, not a change in intrinsic value, and we
already hold it in the lens. No registered source discloses index-product holdings of ALII, so we do
not put a number on the flow.
**Commodity and policy — medium likelihood, medium impact.** Coal export rules and the domestic
market obligation set the miners' budgets and therefore Ancara's tonnage [S11].
**Currency — medium likelihood, medium impact.** The related-party receivable is largely
dollar-denominated, which produced a large FX gain in 9M 2026; a stronger rupiah reverses it [S6].
**Governance — medium likelihood, high impact.** Related-party pricing is set on terms that may not
match third-party terms, as the notes themselves state [S5]. OJK's 2026 sanctions on parties in the
DSSA/BREN/CUAN cases and its statement that such cases can proceed to criminal action [S15][S16] set
the enforcement backdrop; ALII is not named, but a konglo name on the HSC list carries this tail.
**Financing — low likelihood, medium impact.** Leverage is modest and the refinancing is fixed-rate,
but the capex tranche is drawn against future vessel deliveries [S10].

blocks.text: Our business scenarios are mirrored around the same two drivers, revenue growth and gross margin, with probabilities of 25.0% bear, 50.0% base and 25.0% bull, and values of Rp186, Rp232 and Rp306 respectively.

The bear case has the affiliated miners continuing to cut volumes, the partial recovery we assume for FY2027E failing to arrive, and the margin giving back part of the fuel recovery; the bull case has volumes recovering with firm coal prices and the twenty tugboats and six barges under the BRI tranche earning from the second half of FY2027 [S10]. Neither scenario assumes a receivable write-down in the operating value; that risk is discussed above, sized there, and would be additional [S6].

The konglo lens is the second half of the target, and it cuts against the business view. The shares sit on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, with the public (each holder below five per cent) at 20.2% and the registry's free float at 19.4% [S6]. On the business alone we value them at Rp215 over twelve months, against today's fundamental value of Rp199, so the market pays 3.0x the latter on the day we write. The lens does not assume that premium is either worthless or permanent: the only flag it applies is the HSC status, because the float is above the fifteen per cent minimum with no tier step due, the registry records no ALII enforcement and no further deletion, and the HSC exclusion takes effect on 2 November 2026 [S17]; the formalisation is already inside the lens, not a new input. OJK's statement that DSSA/BREN/CUAN-type cases can proceed to criminal action [S16] is a regime reminder; no ALII case is named. With no dated remediation step left, the most likely path is slow compression: in the base regime 35.0% of the log gap closes over twelve months, against -10.0% in the bull regime and 75.0% in the bear. That is what lifts the target to Rp475 from the fundamental value, and it is also why the target remains below the price. If the regime premium re-rates faster than we assume the stock falls toward fundamental value; if the HSC status persists longer than the lens assumes the target is too low, and that is the main way we are wrong on the upside [S17][S16].

Signposts that would change our view: a sourced explanation of the Q3-2026 revenue step-down with evidence of restored tonnage; cash collection of related-party interest rather than further accrual; a reduction in the non-current related-party balance; any ALII-specific OJK action or a further change in the HSC treatment; and the MSCI decision rather than a float requirement this name already meets.

Ancara is a Bakrie-group vehicle: its parent is PT Graha Adika Niaga, and its controller and ultimate beneficial owners are Aburizal Bakrie and Nalinkant Amratlal Rathod [S5]. The group's coal mines are its customers, its head office is in Bakrie Tower, and the affiliated miners were named as the purpose of the company at formation [S4]. The register is concentrated: PT Graha Adika Niaga holds 32.9%, Solomed Capital Pte. Ltd. 31.6% and Borneo Logistics Services Pte. Ltd. 11.0%, while the public, each holder below five per cent, holds 20.2% [S6]. Pending the Director's registry update, the report shows both float measures: the LK's public table of 20.2% at 30 September 2026 as the primary disclosure, and the registry's market-convention free float of 19.4%, which is a slightly narrower measure and carries no date of its own. Both clear the fifteen per cent minimum, so the lens is unchanged either way [S6]. The coverage registry also does not yet carry ALII in the BAKRIE group even though the annual report names PT Graha Adika Niaga as parent and Aburizal Bakrie as controller [S5]; both registry gaps are referred to the Director, since the registry is the Director's file. The lens is read on the name-specific facts, which do not change with the group tag, so the valuation is unaffected. The HSC listing is a disclosure status, not a finding of wrongdoing [S13], and the 2 November IHSG formalisation is already inside the lens [S17].

Related-party dealings are extensive and disclosed: revenue from two affiliates, trade and other receivables from the same parties, a non-current loan book to them, and a payable to another affiliate [S5][S6]. The notes state plainly that related-party terms may differ from third-party terms [S5]. The non-current loan book is close to half of total assets, and in Q3 its interest and penalty income exceeded operating profit [S6]; we value it at a haircut to book in the bridge and hold its income in the non-operating line. Interest accrues at a high coupon with no fixed repayment date on part of the balance, and maturities have been extended by amendment [S5][S6].

OJK's 2026 sanctions list names parties in the DSSA, BREN and CUAN cases, with fines and written orders, and OJK says cases of this type can proceed to criminal action under the una-via principle [S15][S16]. ALII is not named in that list, and the registry records no enforcement against it. We treat it as regime context for the group's cost of capital and float, not as an ALII finding.

Dividend policy allows up to four-fifths of net profit after capex and working capital [S3]; the FY2025 payout was Rp13 per share, a little over two-thirds of that ceiling, and was paid in 9M 2026 [S6]. A controlling shareholder that is also the borrower has a claim on cash that competes with the minority dividend — we watch the receivable balance as the dividend signal.

ESG exposures are those of coal logistics: the fleet's emissions and the environmental risk of barge operations on Kalimantan rivers, plus the social licence of the coal chain itself. The company publishes a sustainability report [S5]; we did not find a quantified emissions target in the filings we registered.

Dated catalysts: the 9M 2026 results, published at the end of October 2026, are already in our numbers [S6]; the HSC exclusion takes effect on 2 November 2026 [S17], with IDX saying the index level is unaffected; the FY2026 audited results and dividend declaration are expected in the first quarter of 2027 [S5]; and the MSCI market-classification decision is due by the end of June 2027, with feedback until the end of April 2027 [S14]. OJK's criminal-action route for DSSA/BREN/CUAN-type cases is a monitoring item, not a dated ALII catalyst [S16].

The KPIs we monitor between updates: monthly tonnage moved and the revenue per tonne implied by the quarterly segment disclosure [S5]; the related-party receivable balance and how much of the interest is collected in cash [S6]; trade receivable days; the gross margin against Brent [S5]; barge deliveries and the capex pace under the BRI capex tranche [S10]; any change in the composition of related-party revenue [S5]; and the reconciliation of the data pack's quarterly operating lines to the LK.

The quarterly cadence is the practical test of our base case. The fourth-quarter report will show whether the weak run-rate of the third quarter was a one-off scheduling gap or the new level: if revenue per tonne recovers while the balance sheet stops absorbing cash, the bull case is live and we would revisit the multiple; if the receivable grows again while tonnage stays weak, the bear case is being delivered and the risk is to the loan book, not to the earnings multiple. The fourth-quarter pack will also be checked line by line against the LK: the Q3 operating-profit and operating-expense lines did not reconcile, and we will not carry a mismatch into the model. We would also treat any related-party contract repricing disclosed in the notes as a change to the revenue base rather than a timing item, because the captive relationship is where the pricing power sits [S5].

bear.narrative: Affiliated miners cut volumes or reprice contracts; the Q3-2026 revenue step-down persists, the partial recovery we assume for FY2027E does not arrive, and the margin gives back the fuel recovery. A receivable write-down is discussed separately and is not one of these two shocks.

bull.narrative: Affiliate volumes recover as HBA firmness feeds mining output; the 20 tugboats and 6 barges under the BRI capex tranche (S10) are delivered and earn from the second half of FY2027, and third-party customers grow. This is also the path a cash repayment of the loan book or a payout toward the 80% ceiling would require.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

adjustments.why: on the exchange's HSC list (as of 2026-10-22): out of the IHSG, the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 and the MSCI indexes [konglo deck S3]

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E = 9M-2026 actual revenue of Rp701.5bn [S6] plus a Q4 at the Q3-2026 run-rate of Rp121.8bn (9M less 1H, [S6]/[S12]) = Rp823.3bn, i.e. -15.1% on FY2025. The pack's Q3 revenue reconciles exactly to that arithmetic. FY2027E +2% is a deliberate ramp, not a full recovery: no filed affiliate tonnage contract or management recovery plan exists [S6], and the 26-vessel BRI tranche is capacity, not committed tonnage [S10]. The year therefore starts near the Q4 trough and accelerates only as utilisation improves; FY2028E +8% completes the recovery once the new tugs and barges are in service. Growth then fades to 6%, 5% and 4% long-run. The same recovery is removed in the bear case.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025 actual 45.4% [S5]; 9M-2026 45.3% [S6] but Q3 alone 30.5% (9M gross profit Rp318.2bn less 1H Rp281.0bn on Q3 revenue of Rp121.8bn, [S6]/[S12]). FY2026E is the 9M actual plus a Q4 at the Q3 gross margin = 43.2%, not a snap-back to the nine-month average. FY2027E 44.0% stages the recovery with the ramp in revenue rather than assuming a full snap-back in one year; FY2028E restores 45.0%, the FY2025 actual, once tonnage is back. Loading-unloading earns a structurally higher margin than barging.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 opex 8.3% of revenue [S5]; 9M-2026 9.5% [S6] but Q3 alone 15.3% (9M opex Rp66.4bn less 1H Rp47.8bn on Q3 revenue of Rp121.8bn, [S6]/[S12]) as revenue fell faster than the fixed cost base. FY2026E is the 9M actual plus a Q4 at the Q3 ratio = 10.3%; FY2027E 10.0% because the revenue ramp is modest while head-office and terminal costs are fixed; then fades to the FY2025 actual 8.5% as the fleet additions absorb fixed cost.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Coal price does not enter the cost base directly: the cost lines are freight, fuel, charter-in, depreciation, loading service and maintenance (S5 note 28). Set to zero; coal prices reach the P&L through customer volumes, not COGS.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: No coal-price cost exposure, so pass-through is nil (S5 note 28 cost composition).

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Fuel is 22.8% of FY2025 COGS (S5 note 28: Rp120.5bn of Rp529.8bn); the tug/barge fleet burns marine fuel that moves with Brent.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Fuel cost is recovered through per-tonne freight rates: the 9M-2026 gross margin (45.3%) held at the FY2025 level although Brent moved from about US$68 to US$96, which shows the recovery in the rate (S5/S6 note 28). Full pass-through keeps the base case at the last actual margin.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 D&A Rp65.9bn = 6.8% of revenue (S5 notes 12/13/28) on a fleet depreciated over 10-20 years; rises modestly as the new barges delivered under the BRI capex facility enter service.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex Rp105bn (10.8% of revenue, [S5] cash-flow statement); 9M-2026 Rp104.5bn already [S6], of which Rp72.6bn fell in Q3 alone as barge construction under the Rp200bn BRI capex tranche accelerated [S6][S10]. FY2026E holds the 9M ratio (14.9%) rather than assuming the Q3 spend stops; it fades as the fleet build completes.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 NWC Rp371.5bn = 38.3% of revenue [S5]/[S6]; 9M-2026 NWC Rp386.2bn on a falling revenue base = 46.9% of FY2026E revenue, dominated by related-party trade receivables [S6]. FY2026E holds the 9M actual ratio rather than assuming a release; it normalises to 38% only as revenue recovers.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Total tax burden FY2025: income tax Rp74.1bn plus the above-the-line tax and final-tax charges Rp16.2bn on PBT Rp496.9bn = 18.2% (S5 note 30b/31). Applied to forecast PBT.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: BRI investment credit signed April 2026 at 7.5% p.a. fixed (S10), replacing Mandiri facilities; the 0.5pp add-on for lease liabilities is dropped because the facility rate is the sourced cost of the drawn debt and leases are a small part of the stack (S6).

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Bank interest income FY2025 Rp1.79bn on minimal cash (S5 note 30a); related-party interest is modelled as non-operating, not as a cash yield.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: 9M-2026 long-term loan receipts Rp294.5bn less repayments Rp252.2bn, plus the lease movement, lifted gross debt from Rp245.2bn to Rp290.5bn [S6]; FY2026E uses that realised step before scheduled amortisation resumes against the Rp200bn BRI capex tranche [S10].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Interest and penalty income accrued on due-from-related-party balances: Rp169.0bn FY2025 and Rp124.6bn in 9M-2026 [S5]/[S6] - an annualised run-rate of about Rp166bn. FX on USD-denominated receivables is EXCLUDED here because it is volatile and non-cash (the 9M-2026 LK shows a Rp61.2bn gain, [S6]); it is discussed in section 3, not forecast. Net of the above-the-line tax charges now carried in tax_rate. The loan book grew from Rp1,160.9bn to Rp1,262.8bn [S6]; no repayment path is sourced, so the line is held at the 9M run-rate rather than faded as the prior version assumed.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025 minorities Rp48.6bn of Rp422.9bn net profit = 11.5% [S5]; 9M-2026 non-controlling interests Rp38.5bn of Rp328.8bn net profit = 11.7% [S6]. FY2026E uses the 9M actual; it eases only slowly as ACT/ATS minorities grow.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 DPS Rp13 on EPS Rp23.65 = 55% (S5); board policy is up to 80% of net profit after capex and working capital (S3). We hold the last actual 55%, not a default haircut: the Rp205.7bn dividend paid in 9M-2026 was the FY2025 payout at 55% (S6), and the controlling shareholder is also the borrower, so cash is more likely retained than paid to the 80% ceiling.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No corporate action announced; shares 15,825.8m (S5, S6).

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Long-run nominal growth in line with Indonesian inflation for a domestic coal-logistics service.

challenges.challenge: The 30%-weighted EV/EBITDA leg (401 vs DCF 238) applies the 12.91x peer median to FY2025A EBITDA of 425.5 - roughly 3x the Q3-2026 annualised EBITDA (~140: Q3 EBIT 18.5 plus D&A) and 1.3x FY2026E 328.1 - and section 4 calls 425.5 'the current earnings base'. For a cyclical in a step-down that is the procyclical error the industry card forbids.
challenges.answer: The EV/EBITDA leg still reads the engine's LTM FY2025A EBITDA because the engine has no forward-metric switch, so we accept by down-weighting it from 30% to 10% and labelling it an optimistic bound: 12.9x peer median on Rp425.5bn peak EBITDA against FY2026E Rp328.1bn. The DCF now carries 70% and P/BV 20%; the weights.changed QC flag is justified with [S0][S6]. After the v4 bridge fix the leg is Rp384.8/share; at the FY2026E metric it would be roughly a fifth lower, in line with the EBITDA gap (peak Rp425.5bn vs FY2026E Rp328.1bn), and the blend now largely ignores that difference.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E holds Q4 at the Q3 run-rate (Rp121.8bn) but FY2027E revenue of 889.2 implies an average quarter of ~222.3 - +82% on that Q4 and ~92% of the FY2025 average - while the basis calls it 'partial normalisation' and management has given no explanation or plan. The 26-vessel BRI tranche is capacity, not a cited tonnage contract.
challenges.answer: FY2027E revenue growth cut from +8% to +2%, gross margin staged at 44.0%, opex held at 10.0%; FY2028E growth +8% and margin 45.0% complete the recovery. No filed affiliate tonnage contract exists, so we ramp instead of assuming a snap-back; the 26-vessel tranche is capacity, not tonnage [S10]. DCF effect, after the v4 bridge fix: target moves from 506 to 477 and the fundamental twelve-month value from 271 to 220.

challenges.challenge: The Rp1,262.8bn loan book (43% of total assets) is added at 100% book with bridge probability 1.0, and section 5 says 'the engine has no bridge-probability override'. That is false: cov_engine.bridge_items weights value x probability, and the assumptions bridge already carries a probability field. The 9M LK shows only Rp46.8bn of the Rp124.6bn interest and penalty income received in cash (S6 p.10 'Penerimaan bunga'), and the loan has no fixed repayment date (21%, 72-month term after amendment).
challenges.answer: Bridge probability set to 0.80 (a twenty per cent haircut) after the QC review, sourced to the 9M cash receipt: only Rp46.8bn of the Rp124.6bn interest and penalty accrued was received in cash [S6 p.10], part of the balance has no fixed repayment date [S5], and the loan book grew in the nine months. The false statement that the engine has no bridge-probability override is removed; §5 says the bridge is already probability-weighted at 80%. The per-share effect is about Rp8/share per 10pp: the bridge counts Rp1,010.2bn, not Rp1,262.8bn.

challenges.challenge: S17 itself says HSC shares are 'dibayangi tekanan jual' and 80 of 962 stocks leave on 2 November; IDX's 'index level unaffected' is about the IHSG arithmetic, not ALII's flow. The report calls it a calendar event that 'removes a marginal buyer' without sizing the 19.4% free float (~3,070m shares, ~Rp1.86trn at Rp605) or daily turnover.
challenges.answer: The float at risk is now sized in §5: the 19.4% public float of 15,825.8m shares inside a Rp9.57tn market capitalisation, against Rp0.9bn three-month average daily turnover - clearing it at recent turnover would take years of trading. This is stated as stock-level discount risk, separate from IDX's statement that the index arithmetic is unaffected. No index-product holding of HSC names is sourced.

challenges.challenge: cov_engine qc shows a -4.00pp FY2025A EBITDA-margin gap (actual 43.85% vs model 39.85%) with no qc_justification; v1 was -0.65pp. The FY2026E trough build therefore fails the house test that FY+1 reproduces the last actual year at that year's prices.
challenges.answer: The calibration gap is -4.00pp (FY2025A 43.85% vs FY2026E 39.85%), below the engine's 5.0pp BLOCK threshold, so no calibration flag exists to answer in qc_justifications and adding one would create an orphan. We still answer it in §3: the gap is the Q3-2026 trough carried into Q4 at the sourced run-rate [S6][S12], and FY2027E/FY2028E restore margin only with the staged revenue ramp, not a snap-back.

challenges.challenge: The update never states the prior target or fundamental. v1 model: tp_final 515.5, tp_fundamental 272.8, DCF 242.6; v2: 505.7, 270.7, 238.3 (-1.9%/-0.8%/-1.8%). The prose ('we have cut the FY2026E gross margin and raised opex and working-capital ratios') reads like a larger reset than a 2% target move.
challenges.answer: The prior target/fundamental bridge is recorded: v1 515.5/272.8, v2 505.7/270.7, revised v4 477/220. Typed numbers are barred from report prose, so the Investment summary states the moves qualitatively (target about seven per cent lower than the prior published level; fundamental about nineteen per cent lower) and the exact bridge is documented here. The components are the FY2027E revenue ramp (-6pp) and margin stage (-1pp), the EV/EBITDA weight cut 30% to 10%, and the bridge haircut 100% to 80%.

challenges.challenge: The base DCF carries FY2026E capex of 122.7 (14.9% of revenue, sourced to the 9M 104.5) for the 20-tug/6-barge BRI tranche but no separately sourced revenue or EBITDA from those assets; the bull adds only the mirror +6pp. Either the capex is replacement (say so) or the base omits the earning asset. The 80% payout ceiling (S3) is also never quantified.
challenges.answer: §3 now states the capex is replacement and fleet renewal plus capacity whose incremental tonnage is not separately sourced, and the bull case carries the 26-vessel tranche earning from H2 FY2027 [S10]. Dividend capacity is quantified: FY2026E yield 1.7% at the modelled 55% payout, proportionally higher at the 80% policy ceiling but still below our cost of equity, so the ceiling is a bull input, not the base case. The §4 anchor statement sets dividend yield against our through-cycle NAV.

challenges.challenge: The summary says related-party interest and penalties reached IDR170.1bn in FY2025; S5 note 30a says 169.023686 (131.458 interest + 35.773 penalty + 1.793 bank interest), and the assumptions basis uses 169.0. The same support metric is quoted two ways.
challenges.answer: Added fact F66 = 169.023686 (S5 note 30a, 'Penghasilan bunga dan denda 169.023.686') and the summary now quotes {{fact.F66|money}} instead of the Rp170.1bn line that mixed in bank interest. The assumptions basis already uses 169.0, and §3 cites the same fact, so one figure runs through summary, basis and section 3.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the after-tax cost of debt reflects the 7.5% fixed BRI facility, but cov_engine sets kd = rf 7.45% + 2.0% debt spread = 9.45% and never reads a.cost_of_debt. The value effect is only ~4.5bp of WACC (~0.4%), but the stated input is not the modelled one and v1 C8 is therefore not actually fixed.
challenges.answer: The engine computes kd as rf plus the default spread (9.45%) and does not read a.cost_of_debt; wiring the sourced 7.5% BRI rate would require a script change we may not make. §4 now states the modelled {{val.coc.kd_pre_tax|pct}} and says the sourced fixed BRI facility rate is lower, so the WACC is if anything conservative. The sentence claiming the cost of debt reflects the fixed BRI rate is removed.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the price is 2.43x 'our fundamental value'; that ratio is 605/248.6 (today's value), while the headline fundamental 12-month value is 270.7, so price/that is 2.23x. Section 5 says 'on the day we write', which is defensible, but the two numbers are never reconciled and the packet prints both.
challenges.answer: §4 and §5 label {{val.konglo.v_fundamental|px}} as today's fundamental value and {{val.tp_fundamental|px}} as the twelve-month value; the premium ratio (now 3.0x after the v4 bridge fix) is explicitly measured against today's value, and the report states the price remains above the twelve-month value. The exact 605/220 ratio is not typed in prose because the no-typed-number law forbids it; the two anchors no longer read as contradictory.

challenges.challenge: other_nonop FY2026E 166.0 equals the 9M interest+penalty 124.6 annualised, so it excludes FX, while the basis says 'plus FX on USD-denominated receivables' and the 9M LK shows a Rp61.2bn FX gain. The number and its stated basis disagree.
challenges.answer: The other_nonop basis now states explicitly that FX on USD-denominated receivables is EXCLUDED because it is volatile and non-cash (the 9M-2026 LK shows a Rp61.2bn gain, [S6]); §3 says the same. The 166.0 line remains the annualised interest and penalty run-rate, so the number and its stated basis now agree.

challenges.challenge: The konglo registry shows ALII groups: [] and the BAKRIE member list excludes ALII, although S5 p.19 names PT Graha Adika Niaga as parent and Aburizal Bakrie/Nalinkant Rathod as controller/UBOs. The report's group treatment is right, but the registry that drives the lens profile is incomplete.
challenges.answer: Confirmed: coverage/universe/konglo.yaml has groups: [] and ALII is absent from BAKRIE, while S5 p.19 names PT Graha Adika Niaga as parent and Aburizal Bakrie/Nalinkant Rathod as controller/UBOs. This is a Director registry fix, not a lens change; §6 now records the gap and states the valuation is unaffected. No group-level enforcement, pledge or related-party event specific to ALII was found in the registry.

challenges.challenge: The industry card requires a dividend-capacity yield versus NAV anchor statement. At the 80% policy ceiling (S3), FY2026E EPS ~19.1 implies DPS ~15.3 (2.5% yield) against the modelled 10.5 (1.7%), and the report never states the yield or which anchor the market uses.
challenges.answer: §3 and §4 now state the dividend-capacity yield: {{mult.FY2026E.div_yield|pct}} at the modelled 55% payout, proportionally higher at the 80% policy ceiling but still below cost of equity. The §4 anchor statement contrasts that yield with our through-cycle NAV anchor. The 80% ceiling is characterised as a plausible bull input, not the base case.

missing_bull_case.note: Bull is a mirror of bear (+6pp growth/+2pp margin) while the Rp200bn BRI tranche's 20 tugs and 6 barges are prose only; the 80% payout ceiling (S3) and its DPS/yield upside are never quantified. See C7 and C13.

missing_bear_case.note: The HSC selling flow is asserted, not sized (S17 itself says 'dibayangi tekanan jual'); the loan book's cash collection (Rp46.8bn of Rp124.6bn 9M) and a recovery haircut are absent; the FY2027E recovery has no sourced tonnage. See C4 and C3.

assumption_realism.note: FY2027E +8% implies ~92% of FY2025 revenue, a near-full recovery from the Q4 trough the model holds; opex 9.5% and gross margin 45% snap back with no sourced tonnage. other_nonop 166.0 excludes the FX gains its own basis claims. See C2 and C11.

evidence_and_citations.note: F26/F27/F37/F38/F44/F45, the controller (S5 p.19), S16 una-via and S17 'tidak memengaruhi nilai IHSG' verify; the peer median 12.91x reproduces (TEBE is the median). But the summary's FY2025 interest+penalty Rp170.1bn is wrong; S5 note 30a says 169.0. See C8.

valuation_method_fit.note: The primary DCF, the no-double-count treatment and the P/BV leg are right, but the EV/EBITDA leg applies 12.91x to FY2025 peak EBITDA at 30% weight, the WACC uses kd 9.45% not the sourced 7.5%, the bridge is 100% though the engine supports probability, and 2.43x uses 249 not the 271 headline. See C1, C3, C9 and C10.

flags.message: interest_income FY2024A restated at 0.03x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The pack's FY2024A interest income of Rp132.45bn is related-party interest of Rp128.25bn plus bank interest of Rp4.20bn [S5 note 30a]; the filing's Rp149.23bn interest-and-penalty total adds the Rp16.77bn related-party penalty, which the pack excludes. The restatement treats the Rp128.25bn related-party accrual as non-operating, so only the Rp4.20bn cash bank interest is left in interest income [S5 note 30a].

flags.justification: The pack's Rp133.3bn interest income is related-party interest of Rp131.5bn plus bank interest [S5 note 30a]; the related-party accrual is classified as non-operating, leaving Rp1.79bn here.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.5, 'ev_ebitda': 0.3, 'pbv': 0.2}
flags.justification: The EV/EBITDA leg is cut to 10% because the engine applies the 12.9x peer median to LTM FY2025A EBITDA of Rp425.5bn, the cycle peak (FY2026E is Rp328.1bn and the Q3-2026 run-rate is far lower), so it is an optimistic bound, not a base weight [S0][S6]. The DCF carries 70% and P/BV 20% (the floor), which is the industry card's through-cycle approach for a cyclical in a step-down.

flags.message: konglo lens: price is 3.04x fundamental value (premium); the base case closes 35% of the log gap in 12 months (hsc); target 475 vs fundamental 12-month value 215 — explain it in §4 and §6
flags.justification: The price is a premium to fundamental value and the base regime closes only part of the log gap because the HSC regime has no dated remediation step left: the float is above the fifteen per cent minimum, no tier step is due and no ALII enforcement exists [S17][S6].
